newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Banoffee coffee to slow UK soft drink shift.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Banoffee coffee to slow UK soft drink shift.

text.p: Britain's coffee industry is fighting sky-high bean prices and a steady consumer shift towards soft drinks with a fast expanding market in exotic-tasting coffee.

Manufacturers of flavoured coffee, ranging from 'banoffee pie' to best-selling 'Irish cream', say they could be the key to attracting people back from trendy carbonated drinks - despite soaring coffee prices.

"Flavoured coffee is definitely on an upward trend," said Cally Affleck a director at Boaters Flavoured Coffee Company -- which has doubled in size every year since opening in 1990. "Coffee does struggle against soft drinks, but the flavoured market is growing and it can definitely fight back."
Consumption of soft drinks in Europe has increased by 60 percent in the last ten years, compared to a two percent rise in coffee.
Brendan Quinn, director at independent Canadean research, said people's habits were changing as they spent less time at home and often ate on the move.
SOFT DRINKS MAKING BIG STRIDES

"The soft drink habit is becoming more of a lifetime thing than a childhood thing and more and more adults are drinking carbonated drinks like cola," he said. "Soft drinks are widely available, and come in bottles which makes them portable and more convenient than hot beverages."
The trend, well-established in the United States and Germany, has been put down to clever marketing.
"The soft drinks companies have very aggressive advertising campaigns using wacky adverts, whereas coffee's image is a bit staid," said Affleck.
But experts say there is potential to lure customers away from fizzy drinks and back to quality ground coffee.

"There is a terrific amount of interest in fresh, quality coffee and it's increasing dramatically," said Leslie Mills, Managing Director of Masteroast, a specialist coffee maker. "And with the increase in the range of flavoured coffees, I can see increasing consumption for quite some time."

Ground coffee retailers, such as the soon-to-be floated Whittards, have introduced enticingly packaged gourmet brands and an increasing range of flavours. And gourmet coffee bars are spreading across Britain from the cosmopolitan capital city.
"We are continually striving to promote fresh coffee," said a Whittards spokeswoman, adding that sales of flavoured coffee had shot up since they were introduced five years ago.
HIGHER PRICES HITTING COFFEE'S COMEBACK
But this year's rally in coffee prices, driven by supply fears after crops were hit by bad weather and threatened strikes, has presented a fresh hurdle.

Robusta type coffee, used in instant coffee which makes up 90 percent of the UK market, rose by 50 percent in the first two months of this year, prompting several European roasters to increase retail prices by 15-20 percent earlier this month.
Ground coffee makers have been even harder hit as the arabica coffee beans they use shot up to $2 a pound - the highest since a severe Brazilian frost in 1994 squeezed supply.

A major coffee retailer told Reuters it was meeting to discuss possible price rises, while a fashionable cafe chain said it had effectively put prices up 20 percent by reducing the size of a cappuccino. With the summer season looming over sales, the pressure for price hikes is set to mount.

George Miller, Chairman of the Beverage Service Association, which represents 85 UK coffee firms, said the worst hit so far were caterers who bought ground coffee, and further hikes in instant brands would probably be led by leading European roaster Nestle.
Experts said although prices had partly been pushed up by speculators, with world coffee supply now finely balanced, there was a fundamental prop behind the prices.
And that is bound to intensify competition from soft drinks.

"It is worrying at these price levels," said one a major European roaster. "I think it's more of a slow erosion rather than a giant bite, but clearly it's a cause for concern and something that needs to be combatted -- and with that sort of aggression, it's not the best time to have prices of this magnitude."
As the first rays of spring sunshine beckon thirsty Britons to street cafes and send waiters scurrying to dust off tables, cola and coffee could be set for a long hard fight this summer.
